ai.literal: For the help done without [the receiver] having done [any prior help], even the earth and even the heaven, matching [it], is rare.
ai.translation: For a help rendered to one who has done no prior favor, even the earth and the heaven are not an equivalent recompense.
ai.modern: முன்பு தான் எந்த உதவியும் செய்யாதிருந்தும் தனக்குச் செய்யப்பட்ட உதவிக்கு, மண்ணுலகத்தையும் விண்ணுலகத்தையும் கைம்மாறாகக் கொடுத்தாலும் ஈடாகாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of unsolicited or initial help. When someone assists us without us having done any prior favor to them, that act of kindness is priceless because it is born out of pure goodwill rather than obligation. The poet states that even gifting the entire earth and the heavens would not be a sufficient return to match such selfless help. The contrast between 'செய்யாமல்' (without doing) and 'செய்த' (done) emphasizes that the absence of a prior debt makes the received help infinitely valuable.

ai.literal: A help done at the crucial time, even though small, is greatly larger than the world.
ai.translation: A help rendered in the hour of need, though small in itself, is far larger than the world.
ai.modern: தகுந்த காலத்தில் செய்த உதவி சிறியதாக இருந்தாலும், அது உலகத்தை விட மிகவும் பெரியதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes that the value of an action is determined by its timing rather than its physical size. The word 'kālattināl' refers to help given at the exact moment of crisis or necessity. Even if such assistance is small ('siṟidu') in material terms, the fact that it saved someone in their hour of need makes it immeasurably vast. Therefore, its worth is declared to be far greater ('māṇap peridu') than the entire earth ('ñālattin').

words.gloss: those who do not weigh or calculate

ai.literal: The benefit not-calculating done help, [its] goodness if-evaluated, greatness ocean-than is-greater.
ai.translation: If one evaluates the true worth of a help rendered by those who did not calculate the return benefit, its greatness is vaster than the ocean.
ai.modern: கைம்மாறு கருதாமல் ஒருவர் செய்த உதவியின் நன்மையை ஆராய்ந்து பார்த்தால், அதன் சிறப்பு கடலை விடப் பெரியதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the immeasurable value of selfless assistance. The word 'பயன்தூக்கார்' refers to those who act without weighing what they might get in return. When we analyze ('தூக்கின்') the inner worth ('நயன்') of such an unconditional act, we find that its spiritual and moral weight ('நன்மை') is far greater than the vastness of the ocean ('கடலின் பெரிது'). The poet uses the image of the ocean to show that selfless help transcends physical boundaries and calculations.

ai.literal: Even if one does a help of the size of a millet seed, those who understand the value will consider it as of the size of a palmyra palm.
ai.translation: Even if the help rendered is as small as a millet seed, those who truly understand its value will cherish it as huge as a palmyra palm.
ai.modern: தினையளவு மிகச்சிறிய உதவியை ஒருவர் செய்தாலும், அதன் பயனை அறிந்தவர்கள் அதனைப் பனையளவு பெரிய உதவியாகக் கருதுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights how the recipients of a favor evaluate its worth. The poet contrasts two well-known objects of vastly different sizes: the tiny millet seed (thinai) and the massive palmyra palm (panai). Those who truly understand the value of gratitude and the timely nature of help (payan terivar) do not look at the physical scale of the assistance. Instead, they magnify even the smallest act of kindness, treating it as a monumental favor.

ai.literal: The help's measure is not the help itself; the help's value is of the measure of the nobility of those who received it.
ai.translation: The value of a help is not determined by the assistance itself; it is measured by the noble character of those who receive it.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் செய்த உதவியின் அளவு, அந்த உதவியின் தன்மையைப் பொறுத்தது அன்று; உதவி பெற்றவருடைய தகுதியின் அளவைப் பொறுத்தது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how the true value of a helpful act is determined. The poet states that the worth of a favor does not lie in its material size or effort. Instead, the true measure of the help is defined by the noble character and gratitude of the person who receives it. A small act of kindness done to a highly virtuous person becomes immense, while a large favor done to an ungrateful person loses its value.

ai.literal: Do not forget the friendship of those free from blemish; do not abandon the friendship of those who became a support in distress.
ai.translation: Never forget the friendship of those who are pure and free from blemish; never abandon the friendship of those who stood as your support in times of distress.
ai.modern: குற்றமற்றவர்களுடைய நட்பை மறக்கக் கூடாது; துன்பம் வந்த காலத்தில் நமக்குத் துணையாக நின்றவர்களுடைய நட்பைக் கைவிடக் கூடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights two kinds of friendships that must be preserved at all costs. First, one must never forget the friendship of pure-hearted people who are free from faults (மாசற்றார் கேண்மை). Second, one must never forsake the friendship of those who acted as a pillar of support (துப்பு ஆயார்) during times of suffering (துன்பத்துள்). The word 'துப்பு' is used here in the sense of strength or support, which perfectly fits the context of receiving help during adversity.

ai.literal: Through the sevenfold seven births also, they will remember, in their distress, the friendship of those who wiped it away.
ai.translation: Through all the sevenfold births of existence, people will cherish the friendship of those who wiped away their distress.
ai.modern: தங்களுடைய துன்பத்தைத் துடைத்தவருடைய நட்பினை, மக்கள் ஏழு வகையான பிறவிகளிலும் நினைத்துப் போற்றுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the enduring nature of gratitude. The phrase 'ezhumai ezhu pirappum' refers to the classical concept of the sevenfold cycle of births, representing eternity or all future lifetimes. The poet states that when someone wipes away ('tudaittavar') another's deep distress ('vizhumam'), that act of friendship ('natpu') is so profound that the recipient will remember and cherish it ('ulluvar') throughout all their future births. It emphasizes that true help received during a crisis creates an immortal bond of gratitude.

ai.literal: Forgetting a benefit is not good; forgetting a harm on that very day is good.
ai.translation: It is not good to forget a benefit; but it is good to forget a harm on the very day it is done.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் செய்த நன்மையை மறப்பது நல்லதல்ல; அவர் செய்த தீமையை அப்பொழுதே மறந்துவிடுவது நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet teaches us how to handle the good and bad deeds of others. It states that forgetting a benefit received is never good, as gratitude must be preserved. On the other hand, if someone does us harm, we should not hold onto anger; rather, it is best to forget that injury immediately, on the very day it occurs. The contrast between holding onto gratitude and instantly letting go of resentment is the core message of this verse.

ai.literal: Even if they do painful things like killing, upon remembering one good deed done by them, [the pain] will disappear.
ai.translation: Even if someone does you harm as painful as murder, all that suffering will vanish the moment you remember a single good deed they did for you in the past.
ai.modern: கொலை செய்வதைப் போன்ற துன்பங்களை ஒருவர் நமக்குச் செய்தாலும், அவர் முன்பு செய்த ஒரு நன்மையை நினைத்துப் பார்த்தால் அந்தத் துன்பங்கள் மறைந்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme power of gratitude in overcoming resentment. The poet uses a powerful comparison: even if someone inflicts a harm so severe that it feels like being killed ('koṉṟu aṉṉa iṉṉā'), we should not harbor hatred. Instead, by actively remembering ('uḷḷa') even a single good deed ('oṉṟu naṉṟu') that person did for us in the past, the pain and anger caused by their massive harm will completely vanish ('keṭum'). This teaches us that gratitude has the strength to dissolve even the deepest grievances.

ai.literal: For those who destroyed any virtue, escape there will be; escape there is not for the man who destroyed a benefit done.
ai.translation: There may be salvation for those who have destroyed any other virtue; but there is no salvation for the person who has destroyed gratitude by forgetting a benefit done.
ai.modern: எந்த அறத்தை அழித்தவர்க்கும் தப்பிப் பிழைக்க வழி உண்டு; ஆனால், ஒருவர் செய்த உதவியை மறந்து அழித்த மனிதனுக்குத் தப்பிப் பிழைக்க வழியே இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the supreme gravity of ingratitude. The author states that even for those who commit the worst sins or destroy other great virtues, there is still a way to redeem themselves or escape ruin. However, for the person who destroys a benefit done to them, there is absolutely no way of escape or redemption. The word 'கொன்ற' (literally 'killed' or 'destroyed') is used powerfully here to mean utterly wiping out or forgetting a good deed, showing that ingratitude is viewed as a fatal moral crime.
